Title: Cross-source POI dedup / entity resolution
Description:
The same laundromat appears in Overture, FSQ, OSM and DCWP. Without dedup the DNCI inflates wherever coverage overlaps — which is itself geographically biased, so the error is not random.

Approach: spatial blocking (~25m) + normalized-name similarity, per category. Emit a survivorship record so counts are auditable.

Description: ~7,400 cells over NYC's ~778 km². Drop water-only hexes; retain partial hexes with land_fraction for edge normalization (threat §7.7).

Description:
MapPLUTO 26v2. Extract ZoneDist1, CommFAR, ResidFAR, BuiltFAR, UnitsRes, YearBuilt; area-weight onto hexes.

REQUIRED CONTROL, not optional. Without commercial zoning capacity in the supply model the underserved tail fills with park edges, industrial zones and cemetery blocks, and the top-20 list is indefensible on first inspection.

Also supplies the dasymetric ancillary surface and the development-headroom term.

Description:
Stations 39hk-dx4f, Entrances & Exits 68hr-j2j7, Hourly Ridership wujg-7c2s.

Use ENTRANCES, not station centroids — a station can be 400m of walking from its own far entrance. Ridership captures transit quality: a 12-route complex is not a single-route stop.

Caveat to record: ridership window is 2020–2024, so 2020–21 levels are pandemic-depressed.

Description:
ACS 5-yr tract → H3 via tobler, dasymetric with PLUTO UnitsRes as the ancillary surface. Plain areal weighting would spread population evenly across parks, rail yards and cemeteries.

Propagate MOEs — do not silently treat tract point estimates as exact (threat §7.8).

Description: Week-1 exit criterion. A crude choropleth of raw POI density per hex. Not the finding — proof the pipeline is real and the joins are right.

Title: Build OSMnx pedestrian walk graph
Description:
network_type='walk', 4.8 km/h (80 m/min).

Extend the graph BEYOND the city boundary so cross-boundary businesses are reachable where they genuinely are — otherwise every edge hex is spuriously underserved (threat §7.7).

Title: Multi-source Dijkstra access engine
Description:
THE performance-critical design decision. Do NOT compute ~7,400 isochrones.

For each of the 15 categories, run ONE multi-source Dijkstra seeded from every POI in that category at once, cut off at threshold distance. Nodes within cutoff are 'served'.

15 traversals instead of 7,400 — minutes not hours, and it makes the 5/10/15-min sweep affordable (45 traversals total).

Emits analysis.hex_access.

Title: Calibrate saturating k_c per category
Description:
s_c = 1 − exp(−n_c / k_c), calibrated so the first reachable establishment scores ≈0.55.

Essentials tighter (k≈1.25 — one grocery is nearly sufficient); food looser (one restaurant in a 10-min walk is thin, not complete). Revisit against observed count distributions. CONTEXT.md open question #2.

Title: DNCI: weighted geometric mean + unit tests
Description:
DNCI = Π (s_c + ε)^w_c, ε = 0.01.

THE METHODOLOGICAL CRUX. An arithmetic mean lets a hex with fifty restaurants and no grocery, pharmacy or laundromat score well — precisely the failure the thesis exists to detect. Only the geometric form punishes zeros.

Tests must include the adversarial case: 50 restaurants + 0 essentials must score LOW. If that test passes under an arithmetic mean, the test is wrong.

Title: Run 5/10/15-minute threshold sweep
Description: 10 min (800m) is the headline. 5 min (400m) and 15 min (1200m) as sensitivity and for comparability with the 15-minute-city literature.

Title: Redefine 'missing' via per-category reach (monotonicity fix)
Description:
QUESTIONS.md D6, CHECKPOINT D33. The 'missing' rule is definitionally broken, not mistuned: a hex is a gap for category c at window w iff (no c within w) AND (c is present within w for ≥80% of walkable hexes) — but reusing one window for both the reach test and the eligibility bar violates MONOTONICITY. Anything absent within 800m is absent within 400m, so a gap at 10 min must survive at 5 min; instead Manhattan hardware gaps vanish at 5 min because hardware's 400m prevalence drops to 51% and the 80% bar simply stops expecting it (D31). The rule fuses two questions that must be separated: (a) how far people normally go for category c — a property of the category; (b) whether this hex is anomalous relative to that norm — a property of the hex.

Fix: give each category a fixed REACH set once from revealed spacing (loci spacing already computes hex-to-nearest distance; e.g. the distance within which ≥80% of populated hexes already have one). A hex is a gap for c iff its nearest c is beyond reach(c) — no global window survives. The 80% bar only sets reach; it is never again an eligibility filter. Apply the same treatment to the 'walkable' eligibility gate (currently ≥12/15 categories present within one window): walkable iff within reach of most categories, each at its own reach.

Acceptance criterion: a MONOTONICITY unit test — tightening any distance parameter (window, reach, or the eligibility bar) may only add gaps, never remove them. The current screen fails this test; the redefinition must pass it.

Threat to validity, must be stated in the output: revealed spacing reflects historical SUPPLY, not demand — a category the whole city under-supplies will look like it 'naturally' spaces wide and its gaps vanish under this rule too. Contrarian review of the reach values is required before trusting them.

Title: Contrarian review of demand.yaml assumed rows and the 0.80 income cutoff
Description:
CHECKPOINT D37: demand.yaml classifies each of the 15 categories as necessity/discretionary to annotate (never filter) the gap screen with a demand_caveat. Only 7 of 15 rows are paper-backed (Meltzer & Schuetz 2012); the other 8 (hardware, bank, clinic, tailor_repair, nails_beauty, hair_barber, laundry, childcare) are owner priors marked evidence:assumed, and the 0.80-of-citywide-mean-income cutoff defining income_class=low is a judgment call carried over from the paper's ZIP-level analysis without re-validation at address level.

D37 requires this review before the annotation ships: demand_caveat stays a table column, NOT rendered on the map, until it passes. Scope: stress-test each assumed row, check whether the 0.80 cutoff produces sensible splits on the address-level income distribution, and check robustness under the paper's own battery (exclude Manhattan, exclude tiny units, alternate cutoffs).

Pushed to Linear 2026-09-05 as GTM-109.

Title: Port demand_caveat annotation to the address-level gap screen
Description:
CHECKPOINT D37 built the demand annotation on the frozen hex screen (gaps.py); D38 made the residential address the unit of analysis (model/address_gaps.py), which does not yet carry the annotation. D49 then REBUILT the annotation: the binary badge is retired, so this port must carry the D49 form and not the thing D37 shipped.

What to port onto analysis.address_gaps, joined tract -> address through analysis.address_demographics (direct join, no apportionment: an address sits in exactly one tract and carries that tract's MOE as-is; never through hex_demographics):
 • income_ratio — the address's tract median household income divided by citywide MEAN household income ($127,894 ± 988, ACS 2023 B19025/B11001 over the five counties, `loci citywide-income`). Continuous, reported as a number.
 • income_ratio_moe — the tract MOE propagated onto that ratio. Median income MOE runs ~27% of the estimate, which is the whole reason the badge died.
 • income_indeterminate — TRUE where the MOE straddles the comparison. Indeterminate is a THIRD state; it must never be folded into 'not low', because that silently resolves every uncertain case in the direction that keeps the gap looking clean.
 • demand_caveat_text — the reader-facing sentence, with the X6 disclaimer appended. Renderers must not truncate it: the disclaimer is its tail. Clinic is excluded from the annotation (D30).

The necessity/discretionary class comes from demand.yaml as D49 rebuilt it — derived from spend.yaml's BLS CEX income elasticity at the 0.35 cut, which is identified (it is the only cut that reproduces all seven Meltzer & Schuetz paper-backed rows), not an owner prior. Do not re-import income_class or the old population-weighted-median denominator; both are superseded. demand_caveat / lead_missing key off the MOE-confident test (income_ratio + income_ratio_moe < 0.80).

NON-NEGOTIABLE and the thing the test must prove: the annotation NEVER changes which (address, category) pairs are gaps and never changes their order. Re-run D37's set-equality test at address level — run the screen with the annotation forced off and assert an identical gap set — and add a rank-stability assertion, because D48 requires graded output that is refined, never filtered. An annotation that reorders leads has become a filter wearing a costume.

No longer gated on GTM-109: that contrarian review is complete and its verdict IS D49.

Reframed 2026-09-09 (D38/D49): ports the continuous MOE-gated annotation via address_demographics; the binary income_class / caveated_missing version is retired and must not be ported.

Pushed to Linear 2026-09-05 as GTM-110.

Done 2026-09-09 (CHECKPOINT D57): shipped as analysis.address_demand, a sibling table keyed by address_id with no write path to address_gaps — the non-filtering guarantee is mechanical, not conventional. MN+BK: 627,439 rows over 281,842 addresses, 107,009 caveated (17.1%), 286,159 income-indeterminate (45.6%); address_gaps checksums byte-identical before and after.

Title: Feed ZBP size bands into D9 and establishments-per-resident into O6
Description:
QUESTIONS D9 asks whether a count/distance gap flag misses quality gaps a size/diversity measure would catch; QUESTIONS O6 needs a category-specific minimum-viable-catchment population. D40 already built the data both need and it sits unused: analysis.zip_category_establishments carries CBP size bands per category per ZIP, and analysis.zip_establishments plus dasymetric ZIP population give establishments-per-resident directly.

Scope: (1) join size-band shares into D9 as a first size/diversity proxy alongside the existing Herfindahl approach; (2) compute establishments-per-resident by category and feed it into O6's minimum-viable-catchment estimate, then express the result the way the screen now consumes it — as a per-category minimum catchment population that the ADDRESS-level reach ratio is read against (a category whose viable catchment exceeds what an address's reach ring contains is a category the screen should not expect there). Low priority — inputs to open research questions, not blocking any shipped deliverable.

The population denominator must NOT come from the frozen hex layer: the existing establishments-per-resident path ran ZIP population off the majority-vote hex->ZIP crosswalk (GTM-108 scope item 3), which D38 retired. Use ZCTA polygons against tract population, or aggregate analysis.address_demographics to ZCTA — either way the denominator is built from tract->address, not tract->hex.

Reframed 2026-09-09 (D38): denominator moves off the hex->ZIP crosswalk; O6's output is stated as an input to the address-level reach ratio.

Pushed to Linear 2026-09-05 as GTM-111.

Title: Density-class / mode-dependent thresholds
Description:
QUESTIONS.md D7, CHECKPOINT D31. Lower Manhattan and car-dependent outer-borough areas should not share one walk window — a 10-minute walk means something different in a district built for foot traffic than in one built for cars. Cheap proxy needing no new data: scale the per-category threshold (from the sibling ticket) by residential density class. Honest version: ACS vehicle ownership per tract (table B25044), depends on an ACS vehicle-ownership ingest; Census key is set.

Note the interaction with per-category thresholds: threshold(category, density_class) is one small parameterization, not two independent sweeps multiplied together — keep it deliberately small (e.g. 2–3 density tiers) to avoid overfitting a matrix nobody can audit by eye.

Title: Persist hex↔business network distances (hex_poi_distance)
Description:
hex_access stored only counts at 5/10/15 min and discarded the Dijkstra results, so every new question (another walk time, distance to nearest, spacing, the Google coverage comparison) meant a two-minute graph recompute — and the threshold could not be swept.

Now: analysis.hex_poi_distance holds every (hex, canonical business) pair within 30 min with its network distance; hex_access is DERIVED from it in SQL so the two cannot disagree. gaps, spacing and the sweep read the table. `loci score` builds it.

DONE 2026-09-02 — 16.2M rows, ~3 min; derived hex_access matched the previous build row-for-row (229,133 rows; 461,421 / 1,880,500 / 4,235,014 pairs). Nearest-of-category per hex now answers in 60 ms.

Title: SHIP W2: the DNCI map
Description: Week-2 exit criterion and the first genuinely interesting artifact. Sequential palette. Sanity-check against local knowledge before proceeding to E3.

Title: Fit the supply model
Description:
DNCI ~ pop_density + median_hh_income + transit_access + commercial_zoning_capacity + land_fraction + borough FE.

Check prediction P1: the residual must have meaningful spread. If R² > 0.9 there is nothing left to explain and the thesis has no room to be true — report that honestly rather than tuning until it isn't.

Title: Moran's I + spatial error/lag model
Description:
MANDATORY, not optional. Compute Moran's I on residuals; if significant (it will be), re-estimate with pysal spreg and report both.

OLS standard errors on gridded urban data are wrong. Shipping a p-value without this is shipping a p-value you cannot defend.

Title: Residual extraction + opportunity score
Description:
opportunity = (−u_h)⁺ × transit_access × (ResidFAR − BuiltFAR)⁺.

Underserved AND transit-connected AND room to build. Any one of the three missing disqualifies the hex.

Title: LODES WAC annual panel loader 2002–2023
Description:
NY state WAC files, target NAICS 4451/4461/7224/7225/8121/8123/4441/6244. Block-level, 22 vintages.

Blocked on the LODES8 block-vintage verification (E1).

Title: LODES block → hex apportionment
Description:
Areal apportionment of block-level jobs onto H3 cells.

Document the proxy assumption loudly: LODES counts JOBS, not establishments. A ten-employee supermarket and a one-employee laundromat are not comparable units (threat §7.4).

Title: Quantify pre-2020 LODES allocation bias
Description:
Discovered while resolving the LODES vintage check.

LODES8 puts every year on 2020 blocks, but historical years got there by ALLOCATION, not observation: when a 2010 block splits, each job is assigned to a child block at random with probability proportional to AREA share. Census: 'the allocation is a statistical process and may not result in a distribution of jobs that exactly matches the areal distribution.'

Area-proportional is a poor assumption in NYC — a block splitting into a park half and a commercial half spreads jobs by area, putting employment in the park.

This is BIAS, not noise: the error concentrates where blocks were split, blocks split where development happened, and development is the outcome variable.

Size the exposure, test whether H3 res-9 aggregation actually absorbs it, and if not restrict the strongest claims to 2020+ observed data. CONTEXT.md threat 7.4(b).

CANCELED 2026-09-05 (CHECKPOINT D38, Linear GTM-63): hex geography retired; sizes bias in the pre-2020 LODES panel built for the E3 causal/growth chain, which already ran and returned its rejected result — no address-level equivalent.

Description:
Correlate the 2023 LODES cross-section against 2023 DOHMH/DCWP establishment counts per hex. Report the correlation.

This is what licenses the jobs→establishments proxy. Without it the whole panel rests on an unexamined assumption.

Description:
Δlog population, Δlog households (ACS); Δlog ZORI (Zillow, ZIP→hex); permitted residential units (DOB/HPD).

ZIP→hex crosswalk by population weighting — CONTEXT.md open question #4. Label rent as the weakest of the four outcomes in the memo and mean it.

Title: Main growth regression (prediction P2)
Description:
Δy_{h,t0→t1} = β·u_{h,t0} + γ'X_{h,t0} + α_borough + ε, t0=2013 t1=2023.

P2 predicts β < 0 (more negative residual → more subsequent growth). A null or wrong-signed result is a real answer: it would mean gaps persist because they reflect durable demand suppression, not latent opportunity. Report it either way.

Title: Pre-trend test (2003→2013)
Description:
Estimate the same spec on the PRIOR decade. If u_2013 also 'predicts' 2003→2013 growth, parallel trends is broken and the causal reading is unavailable.

Report it whichever way it comes out. This is the check a serious reader will ask for first.

Title: Placebo outcome
Description: An outcome with no plausible mechanism — e.g. change in share of population aged 65+ — must return a null. If it doesn't, the specification is picking up generic neighborhood trajectory rather than the retail channel.

Title: MAUP sweep at res 8 and res 10
Description:
Re-run the whole chain at two other resolutions; report coefficient stability. If conclusions flip with grid size, say so plainly (threat §7.3).

Description:
Tier weights (0.40/0.20/0.25/0.15) are judgment, not derived. Sweep plausible alternatives and report whether the top-20 list is stable under reweighting. CONTEXT.md open question #1.

Title: Top-20 list + zoning-artifact audit
Description:
Produce the ranked list of transit-rich underserved hexes.

HARD GATE: manually inspect for park edges, industrial zones and cemetery blocks. Any present means the commercial-zoning control failed — fix the model, do not hand-remove the rows.

Also check it contains ≥3 genuine surprises. A list of only obvious places means the residual isn't doing any work.

Title: Spacing and nearest-missing distance diagnostics
Description:
QUESTIONS.md D5. Two read-only diagnostics the gap screen cannot answer on its own: (1) nearest-neighbour distance between businesses of the SAME category — how clustered each trade is and how often a business has no competitor within a walk; (2) for each gap hex, straight-line distance to the nearest business of its lead-missing category — separates marginal 10-minute gaps from real holes.

Description:
QUESTIONS.md T5 — does the gap close on its own?

Over 2002–2023, do hexes with a negative residual at t converge toward their peers by t+k (retail employment growth regressed on the lagged residual, borough FE)?

Why it matters: if the market already corrects undersupply, the opportunity is TIMING, not location — a different product and a different memo. Cheap once the LODES panel exists; pull forward if W3 has slack, otherwise it slides to Phase 5.

Title: Retail lead/lag timing test
Description:
QUESTIONS.md T6 — does retail lead or lag rooftops?

Cross-correlate annual per-hex changes in LODES retail employment with changes in population at leads and lags of 1–5 years.

Why it matters: 'retail follows rooftops' is the assumption the whole residual design rests on (D1). This is the one place it gets tested rather than asserted.

CAVEATS to state: ACS 5-year smoothing limits timing resolution to roughly half-decades; LODES counts jobs, not storefronts (M2).

CANCELED 2026-09-05 (CHECKPOINT D38, Linear GTM-65): hex geography retired; tests the D1 assumption underlying the abandoned hex residual design — no address-level equivalent.

Title: SHIP W3: empirical result + top-20
Description:
Week-3 exit criterion.

CANCELED 2026-09-05 (CHECKPOINT D38, Linear GTM-46): hex geography retired; ships the E3 hex residual coefficient and top-20, retained only as honest negative science, not the product. The address-level ranked list is a separate, already-shipped deliverable (D44).

Title: Design stratified coverage validation sample
Description:
Prediction P3 and threat §7.1 — the one that can invalidate everything.

OSM/Overture undercount small business in lower-income and immigrant neighborhoods: exactly the areas the thesis flags as underserved. If the undercount is strong there and weak in Park Slope, the 'retail gap' is a data gap wearing a costume.

Draw hexes at random within each income decile, and cross-stratify by foreign-born share (ACS) so borough / immigrant-neighborhood contrasts in the residual (QUESTIONS.md X3) can be separated from coverage bias. Fix n per stratum against the 5,000-call budget before spending anything.

DONE 2026-09-02 — src/loci/validation/sample.py: NTILE(10) on median income among populated hexes, seeded random draw per decile, like-for-like 800 m straight-line counts for Google vs Overture/OSM/anchor. Foreign-born cross-stratification NOT possible yet: hex_demographics has no foreign-born column (add to ACS ingest first). Default plan: 200 hexes × 15 categories = 3,000 calls, inside the free tier.

Title: Run Google Places ground-truth enumeration on sampled gap addresses
Description:
Enumerate ground truth for a stratified sample of gap ADDRESSES drawn from analysis.address_gaps. The sampling frame is the address itself, not a hex centroid standing in for one (D38); scope is Manhattan + Brooklyn (D48). Title: Google type-map audit per category
Description:

The 2026-09-03 Google validation run showed raw survival rates (hardware 58%, fitness 29%, clinic 0%) were mostly measuring how much WIDER or NARROWER Google's included type is than loci's category definition, not measuring coverage — a cheap verification that would have de-risked the whole $-budgeted run if done first.

Title: Fitness anchor source for the ~20% true coverage hole
Description:
QUESTIONS.md M7. D29 found a real ~21% [95% CI 10–37] true-coverage-hole rate for fitness after removing the geometry artifact (loci's canonical layer already had a business inside the 800m network radius but outside the validator's straight-line circle). Fitness has no anchor today — OSM/Overture/Foursquare are all general-purpose POI sources carrying the same undercount bias the project exists to correct for, and none is a near-census the way DOHMH is for food or SNAP is for grocery. D37 already flags fitness as the category most weakened by the demand annotation (on the frozen hex screen, 42% of window-rule fitness gaps sat below the low-income line, where the literature says gyms follow income rather than signalling a supply gap); per D49 that annotation is now continuous and MOE-gated and must be recomputed on addresses (GTM-110), but the reading does not change.

That does not weaken the case for finding an anchor; fitness having no near-census is true regardless of the rate.

Candidates to evaluate: a NYS business registry cut for fitness/gym SIC/NAICS codes, DOHMH (if it licenses any fitness-adjacent facility), or state gym/health-club contract-law registration (verify whether NY requires it and whether the file is bulk-accessible).

Scope: (1) rerun `loci zbp-compare` split by source (DOHMH / NYS DOS / NYS SLA / OSM / Overture) to attribute which feed drives each category's overcount; (2) decide whether SLA and NYS DOS anchors need an active-license filter like DOHMH's; (3) add ZCTA polygons for a proper POI→ZIP join, replacing the current majority-vote hex→ZIP crosswalk. Title: Validator: network distance or circuity correction
Description:
QUESTIONS.md M8. D29's GEOMETRY-artifact category (Google found the business AND loci's canonical layer already had it, just outside the validator's straight-line radius but inside the true 800m network-walk radius — median network distance for these hexes ~850m, IQR 830–930) exists because the validator compares Google results against a straight-line circle while the gap screen itself thresholds on NETWORK distance (analysis.hex_poi_distance). The two geographies disagree by construction, which is why every validation result needed a manual geometry/coverage split after the fact.

Two fixes to evaluate: (a) have the validator query analysis.hex_poi_distance directly instead of a straight-line radius, so the comparison uses the same geography as the screen; or (b) keep the straight-line radius but apply a circuity correction (NYC's street network runs ~1.25–1.3x straight-line distance, so an 800m network threshold corresponds to roughly a 620–640m straight-line radius). Either removes the need to hand-split future validation runs. Low priority: the current manual split (D29) already works, this just automates it.

Title: Methodology memo
Description:
The document a skeptic attacks and you defend. What it now documents is the ADDRESS-level gap screen (analysis.address_gaps + analysis.address_demographics, D38) — the hex tables are frozen history and the memo should not read as though they are the product.

Must state plainly:
 • The unit and the rule: a per-category reach screen over residential addresses, reach values from reach_tiers.yaml and the ranking continuous (D41), scoped to Manhattan + Brooklyn (D48). Output is GRADED — every lead carries a grade, none is filtered out — so the memo must show the full ranked surface rather than a shortlist that hides the marginal cases.
 • The reach values come from revealed SPACING, i.e. historical supply, so a category the whole city under-supplies looks like it 'naturally' spaces wide. That is the screen's central circularity and it belongs in the memo, not in a footnote.
 • Coverage bias (§7.1): what the fixed-harness validation showed, which categories are still uninterpretable (clinic, D30/D50), and the ZBP overcount in license-anchored categories (D40) that biases those reach values tight.
 • The demand annotation is continuous, MOE-gated, and NON-FILTERING (D37/D49), with the X6 disclaimer in the reader's own words: it says the literature expects lower discretionary demand here, never that the gap is false.
 • The rejected causal thesis, kept and labelled: the residual design reduced but did not eliminate endogeneity (§7.2), no instrument was used, pre-trends broke, and the retail-gap-predicts-growth coefficient came out wrong-signed (§0/D1). It ships as an honest negative result, never as a claim the product rests on.

Claiming cleaner identification than exists is the fastest way to lose an investment reader.

Title: Charter the premium-amenity axis (CONTEXT §11)
Description:
Owner add 2026-09-02: screen NYC for where a PREMIUM, destination amenity could open — padel courts and spa/wellness studios first.

Why this needs its own charter section and cannot reuse the daily-needs gap screen: the two goods behave oppositely.
 • Daily needs are convenience goods — consumed often, near-zero willingness to travel, so the geography is the 800 m walk and the screen is 'present in ≥80% of walkable peers, absent here.'
 • Premium amenities are DESTINATION goods — consumed occasionally, high ticket price, people will drive/transit 15–30 min for them (the owner's own premise). They are RARE by nature, so a prevalence-gap screen would flag almost everywhere and mean nothing.

So the method inverts to a classic trade-area / gravity site-selection model: a travel-time CATCHMENT with enough qualifying premium demand but little or no supply within that catchment, plus a feasible large-format site. Document it as CONTEXT §11 and CHECKPOINT D22. This is Axis 3, parallel to Axis 1 (Investability, invest.py) and Axis 2 (Rising, rising.py) — NOT a return to the rejected residual-growth thesis (D1).

Title: Define the premium-amenity bundle + demand-target per category
Description:
Padel and spa are the two named anchors; extend to the destination-amenity family that shares the travel-for-it behavior, each kept as its OWN category because catchment size, demand target and site needs differ: padel, spa / day-spa, med-spa, pilates / reformer, boutique fitness / boxing, climbing gym, bathhouse / sauna, golf & sports simulator.

Each category carries (a) its demand TARGET — not raw population: padel skews affluent + athletic + 25–44; med-spa skews affluent women 30–55; climbing skews younger + college-educated — and (b) a nominal catchment travel time and site footprint. These are judgment calls, stated explicitly and tunable, exactly like the daily-needs tier weights and the invest.py ECON minimums (D18). Emit the bundle as data (a PREMIUM dict mirroring ECON), not hard-coded in the scorer.

Title: Ingest premium-amenity supply + Google-validate (mandatory here)
Description:
These amenities are OUTSIDE the daily-needs 15, so they need their own supply layer. Sources: OSM (padel = leisure=pitch + sport=padel; spa = leisure=spa / shop=beauty+beauty=spa; climbing = sport=climbing; sauna = leisure=sauna), Foursquare leaves (Spa, Pilates Studio, Climbing Gym, Boxing Gym, Gym and Studio subtypes), Google Places for ground truth.

Why Google validation is load-bearing here, not optional as it is for daily needs: padel barely existed before 2022 and boutique studios open fast, so OSM/Foursquare snapshots undercount them SEVERELY and unevenly. A padel 'gap' is far more likely to be a data gap than a daily-needs gap is (threat: the §7.1 coverage bias, but worse). Validate every candidate site's catchment against Google + a manual web check before it ships. Reuse the budget-guarded validation client (src/loci/validation/).

Title: Travel-time catchment engine (drive + transit isochrones)
Description:
Replaces the 800 m walk ring with a per-amenity travel-time CATCHMENT — the load-bearing modeling choice for this axis, and the owner's core premise ('people will travel longer').

Build drive-time isochrones (car network) unioned with transit-time where the amenity is transit-oriented (a Manhattan spa is reached on foot/subway; an outer-borough padel box is reached by car with parking). Default 15 min, and because willingness-to-travel is ASSUMED not measured, sweep 10 / 15 / 20 / 30 min and report how the site ranking moves — the sensitivity IS the honesty here. Reuse the OSMnx graph machinery from E2; the drive network and isochrone reach are the new parts.

Emits a catchment membership table keyed candidate SITE × residential address (address_id) — the same unit as the daily-needs screen (D38), so catchment demand aggregates real rooftops instead of population smeared across a grid cell that a 15-minute isochrone clips arbitrarily. Supply joins the same way: reachable premium establishments per site, not per cell.

Reframed 2026-09-09 (D38): catchment membership is site × address, not site × hex.

Title: Premium demand pool per catchment
Description:
Score each catchment's DEMAND — not raw homes (that is the daily-needs driver) but a premium demand pool: population weighted toward the top income deciles, the category's target age band, and college/education share (which D20 already computes and found correlated 0.72 with income). Per-category weighting from the demand TARGET defined in the bundle ticket.

Re-use analysis.address_demographics (income, renter — joined tract -> address directly, no apportionment, per D38) plus the ACS momentum module's age/education pulls (model/momentum.py); do NOT read hex_demographics, which the address pipeline no longer maintains. Sum over the address members of each catchment from the sibling catchment-membership table.

Carry the tract MOE through rather than treating point estimates as exact, and mark a catchment's pool indeterminate where the MOE will not support the ranking — the same discipline D49 imposed on the daily-needs demand annotation. A premium site list ordered by a difference smaller than its own margin is a ranking of noise.

Output: qualifying-demand headcount and $ per candidate catchment, comparable across amenities.

Reframed 2026-09-09 (D38/D49): demographics come from address_demographics, not hex_demographics, and the pool carries its MOE.

Title: Large-format feasibility gate
Description:
The invest.py feasibility gate (D18) but re-tuned for destination formats. A padel court needs ~1,000+ m² and height (warehouse, parking deck, flex/industrial — often NOT a ground-floor retail bay); a day-spa needs mid-size retail or upper-floor; a climbing gym needs a tall shell. So the PLUTO test changes from 'any CommFAR>0 storefront' to lot size + floorplate + a zoning district that permits commercial recreation / personal-service, plus vacancy/industrial-conversion candidates.

Without this the screen recommends amenities onto lots where they physically or legally cannot go — the D3 zoning-artifact failure in a new costume. Gate each candidate site on a buildable/leasable large-format space before it can rank.

Title: Premium opportunity score + ranked site list
Description:
Combine: opportunity = qualifying demand pool in the catchment − existing supply reachable within that catchment, gated on a feasible large-format site, ranked per amenity.

Three threats to state plainly on the list, because a reader will raise them:
 • Supply undercount is worse for these new categories (padel especially) — every top site must survive Google + manual validation or it is presumed a data gap, not an opportunity.
 • Willingness-to-travel is assumed; the catchment radius is the biggest lever, so report the ranking under the 10/15/20/30-min sweep, not a single radius.
 • National-chain pipeline (Life Time, Equinox, Padel Haus, etc.) may already have a site under LOI — outside the data, flagged as manual diligence per top pick.

Produces the padel and spa shortlists the owner asked for.

Title: SHIP: 'Where could a padel court / spa go?' map layer
Description: Axis-3 deliverable, parallel to the invest/rising buy-list artifacts. A map layer (toggle per amenity) showing travel-time catchments shaded by UNMET premium demand, with feasible large-format sites pinned and each top site carrying its demand pool, nearest existing supply, and the validation result. Load the `dataviz` skill before writing chart code.

Title: Charter the maturity + projection axis (CONTEXT §12), honestly vs §0/D1
Description:
Owner add 2026-09-02, two linked questions: (1) where is each neighborhood on its MATURITY curve today, and (2) where could growth get to by 2033 — how do we project it.

This is the forward extension of Axis 2 (Rising, D19/D20/D21), and it MUST be framed to not revive the project's central rejected result. Be explicit in CONTEXT §12:
 • DEAD and staying dead (§0/D1): 'the retail gap/residual at t0 predicts subsequent residential growth' — β was wrong-signed (+0.069), pre-trends broken. This axis never uses the retail residual as a growth predictor.
 • LEGITIMATE and different: locating a neighborhood on a development S-curve from its OWN observed multi-metric history (income, college, rent, permits, jobs), then EXTRAPOLATING that trajectory. The pre-trend finding — that these places are on a development cycle — is precisely what licenses extrapolation.
 • The honesty is in the caveats: extrapolation assumes the frontier keeps diffusing and no macro shock intervenes. D21 already caught ENY rents COOLING to +1.9%/yr — trajectories bend, so the output is scenario bands, never a point forecast, and it is credible only if it passes the backtest ticket.

Retail (Loci's core product) attaches at the END as the dependent read: given a projected 2033 demand surface, today's Axis-1/Axis-3 sites can be re-scored forward. Write CONTEXT §12 + CHECKPOINT D23.

Title: Assemble the multi-decade neighborhood trajectory panel
Description:
momentum.py (D20) pulled only two points (2013 & 2023). Staging and projection need a real time series per NTA. Assemble: decennial 2000 + 2010, ACS 5-yr 2009/2013/2018/2023 (real HH income via B19025/B11001, college share B15003, tenure, age bands), LODES WAC 2002–2023 (already downloaded), Zillow ZORI/ZHVI 2000– (D21), DOB/HPD permit pipeline by year.

Deflate every dollar series to 2023 real (CPI ×1.308 for 2013→2023 per D20 — extend the factor to each vintage) or the trend is mostly inflation. Aggregate each vintage to 2020 NTA via that year's tract centroids (the momentum.py gazetteer method). Output: analysis.nta_trajectory, one row per NTA per year per metric. This is the raw material for BOTH the maturity classifier and the projection.

Title: Neighborhood maturity-stage classifier
Description:
Place each NTA on the development S-curve. THE methodological point: stage is defined by LEVEL and RATE and ACCELERATION (1st + 2nd derivative) of the panel metrics, not by level alone — that is what separates a maturity model from a static wealth map. A high-income but decelerating neighborhood is 'maturing'; high-income and still accelerating is 'rising'.

Stages: pre-frontier/dormant (low level, flat) → emerging (income accelerating, college still low, first permits — where ENY sits: +42% income but college only 9→14%, D21) → rising (income+college both climbing fast, rent + permit boom) → maturing (high level, growth decelerating — Williamsburg now) → mature/saturated (high, flat or declining — the 5 rich Manhattan NTAs in real decline, D20). Spatial adjacency to the already-risen frontier is a feature (gentrification diffuses to neighbors). Output: each NTA's stage + a 0–1 position along the curve.

Title: Frontier-diffusion map: where the edge moved, where it goes next
Description:
Half of 'where could growth get to' is spatial. Trace the observed gentrification frontier 2000→2023 — Williamsburg → Bed-Stuy → Bushwick → Crown Heights → Ocean Hill → East New York (D20 already found this path) — as a datable wave, and identify the not-yet-risen neighborhoods ADJACENT to today's rising edge as the mechanistic next steps.

This is the most communicable form of the forecast and the one most tied to an actual mechanism (diffusion to neighbors), so it anchors the more model-driven projection. Report the frontier's measured pace (blocks/decade) — that pace is what sets the 2033 reach.

Title: 2033 trajectory projection with scenario bands
Description:
Project each NTA's income / college / rent to 2033. Two complementary methods, reported together:
 • Per-metric LOGISTIC (saturating) extrapolation — logistic not linear, because a neighborhood cannot gentrify past 100% and linear extrapolation of a hot decade is the classic forecasting error.
 • Stage-transition (Markov) roll-forward — estimate P(stage→stage per decade) from the historical panel, then advance each NTA one step to 2033, giving a probabilistic stage.

Output is SCENARIO BANDS, never a point estimate: continued-diffusion / stall / reversal, motivated by the live evidence that trajectories bend (ENY rents cooled to +1.9%/yr post-2022, D21). Also produce the analogue read — for each emerging NTA, the already-matured NTA it most resembles at the same stage (ENY-2023 ≈ Bushwick-2011?) and that analogue's realized path as an interpretable forecast.

Title: Backtest the projection (fit 2000→2013, predict 2013→2023)
Description:
The load-bearing credibility check — the analogue to E3's pre-trend/placebo rigor, and the reason this axis is not astrology. Fit the classifier + projection on data through 2013 ONLY, project 2013→2023, and compare to what actually happened. If the model cannot retrodict the Bushwick/Crown Heights/ENY arc it demonstrably cannot forecast 2033, and the memo must say so.

Report out-of-sample error by stage (emerging neighborhoods are the hardest and the most important). This ticket gates whether the 2033 numbers ship as a forecast or only as a scenario illustration.

Title: Bridge to the product: forward-looking demand for Axes 1 & 3
Description:
Close the loop WITHOUT reviving D1. Take the projected 2033 demand surface (population/income/education by scenario) and re-score the Axis-1 investability leads (from analysis.address_gaps, address-level per D38) and Axis-3 premium sites against it, so an address that is marginal on today's demand but sits in a neighborhood projected to mature by ~2030 becomes visible as a forward bet.

Guardrail, stated in code and memo: retail is the DEPENDENT variable of the projection (projected rooftops/income drive projected demand), never the predictor of growth. The moment a retail gap is used to predict neighborhood growth, this has become the rejected thesis again.

Reframed 2026-09-05 per CHECKPOINT D38 (address-level geography). Linear GTM-83.

Title: SHIP: maturity + 2033 projection artifact
Description: Axis-4 deliverable. Per-neighborhood: its position on the S-curve, its 2033 scenario cone (continued/stall/reversal), and its nearest historical analogue; plus the frontier-diffusion map showing where the edge goes next. Every projected number carries its backtest error. Load the `dataviz` skill before writing chart code.

Title: Charter the second-city feasibility screen
Description:
Owner question 2026-09-02: 'are there other cities with data rich enough to do similar work?' Charter the answer before building it, because the naive answer ('big cities have open data') screens on the wrong thing.

What NYC actually gives Loci, decomposed:
 • The POI layer — Overture, Foursquare, OSM, and the OSMnx walk graph — is ALREADY global and free. It ports to any city at ~zero cost and is NOT the constraint.
 • The three crown jewels ARE the constraint, and they are what a second city must reproduce:
   1. An UNBIASED near-census business anchor to correct OSM's undercount in low-income/immigrant areas (DOHMH restaurant inspections — CONTEXT §7.1, 'the project's best asset'). Without it the gap finding is coverage bias in a costume — the P3 threat that can invalidate everything.
   2. Parcel- or grid-level land use (MapPLUTO) — the dasymetric backbone that puts population where housing actually is, plus the commercial-zoning-capacity control that keeps the top list off park edges.
   3. Fine-grained demographics + transit QUALITY (ACS + MTA ridership, not mere station presence).

So the screen scores candidate cities on those three axes (anchor / land-use / demographics+transit), not on 'has an open-data portal.' Write this as CONTEXT §13 and CHECKPOINT D24. This milestone is research + city SELECTION; the universal-interface engineering that actually runs `loci run --city X` is the existing E5 ticket.

Title: Define the city-feasibility rubric as data (CITIES dict)
Description:
Emit the rubric as data — a CITIES dict mirroring how ECON (D18) and the E6 PREMIUM bundle externalize judgment — not hard-coded in prose. Each candidate city scored 0–3 on four axes, each axis naming the CONCRETE analog dataset (not 'they probably have zoning'):
 • anchor — an unbiased near-census business/establishment registry. 3 = all-industry geocoded register (Paris SIRENE, London Companies House); 2 = food+licenses near-census (NYC DOHMH, Chicago business licenses, UK FSA); 1 = licenses only; 0 = none, OSM is all you have.
 • land_use — parcel-level or gridded. 3 = published gridded population (NL CBS 100 m, Japan mesh, Nordic registers) which REMOVES the dasymetric step entirely; 2 = parcel cadastre + zoning (NYC PLUTO, UK OS, most US assessors); 1 = coarse zoning polygons; 0 = none.
 • demographics — 3 = finer than US tracts (UK output areas, INSEE IRIS, ABS SA1, register-based); 2 = US-tract-equivalent (ACS, StatCan DA); 1 = coarse only.
 • transit — 3 = GTFS + ridership/tap data (TfL Oyster, MTA); 2 = GTFS only; 1 = none.

The rubric is judgment stated explicitly and tunable, exactly like the tier weights. Score is min-gated, not summed: a city with a 0 anchor cannot be rescued by great transit, because the anchor is the load-bearing asset.

Title: Verify the universal layer actually runs outside NYC
Description:
Per the CLAUDE.md habit 'verify before committing to a dependency': prove the universal core runs on a non-NYC bbox BEFORE designing the multi-city screen around the claim that it does. Pull a small Overture + OSM + OSMnx-walk-graph extract for one foreign bbox (a few km² of central London or Paris) and confirm: the Overture category map still resolves, the walk graph builds, and the H3 grid clips. Record which of the 15 daily-needs categories lose their anchor once DOHMH/SNAP/SLA/DCWP are gone — that gap IS the coverage warning the second city ships with (see the E5 second-city ticket). Cheap, and it de-risks the whole milestone.

DONE 2026-09-05 (CHECKPOINT D45, Linear GTM-89) — verified on a central London bbox with real Overture/Overpass/OSMnx calls. PASS: category mapping, dedup, walk graph (all ran unmodified). PASS-with-monkeypatch: Overture/Overpass adapters (BBOX/CACHE_PATH are module constants). NOT RUNNABLE: grid/build.py hard-requires nyc_nta2020.geojson + EPSG:2263. Anchor loss: 7 of 15 categories (restaurant, cafe_bakery, bar, hair_barber, nails_beauty, grocery, convenience) lose their near-census anchor outside NYC. Verdict: partially universal, fixes are constant-level not logic-level — see the follow-up ticket below.

Title: Parameterize the universal layer by city (GTM-89 findings)
Description:
GTM-89's second-city dry run found the universal layer is universal in LOGIC but NYC-hardcoded in CONSTANTS. None of the findings are algorithmic blockers — they are places an NYC default was written as a module constant instead of a parameter.

Checklist (from GTM-89, CHECKPOINT D45, minus the items D38 made moot): sources/universal/overture_places.py BBOX/CACHE_PATH → constructor args; sources/universal/osm_overpass.py BBOX → constructor arg; sources/universal/foursquare_places.py same; the NYC region vocabulary (borough / nta_code) carried on addresses → generic region_label / subregion_code, so model/conveniences.py and model/address_gaps.py stop requiring NYC words; score/dedup.py source_rank() takes an injectable per-city anchor map; and the ADDRESS LAYER itself needs a per-city source — NYC gets its residential addresses from PLUTO, and a second city must name an equivalent register. That last item is now the real portability question, and it did not exist when this checklist was written.

Dropped from the checklist 2026-09-09: grid/build.py build_grid(con, boundary_path, proj_epsg, res) and its NYC EPSG:2263 / nta2020 defaults. D38 retired the H3 grid as the unit of analysis, so parameterizing the grid builder buys portability for nothing the project ships — it would only make a frozen table rebuildable elsewhere.

Reframed 2026-09-09 (D38): grid-builder items dropped; per-city address sourcing added as the actual gap. Still parked per D46 — a wording fix, not a scheduling change.

Parked 2026-09-05 — owner decision: NYC focus for the foreseeable future (CHECKPOINT D46). Do not schedule.

Pushed to Linear 2026-09-05 as GTM-104 (Low priority, not blocking).

Title: Candidate-city data dossiers
Description:
One dossier per shortlisted city, each naming the specific dataset behind every rubric axis so the score is auditable, not vibes. Shortlist and the anchor that earns it:
 • Paris / France — SIRENE, the national register of EVERY establishment, geocoded with NAF industry codes; INSEE census at IRIS level; open cadastre. Arguably a BETTER anchor than NYC (all industries, not just food).
 • London / UK — FSA food-hygiene ratings (food near-census) + Companies House (all companies); ONS 2021 census at output-area level (finer than US tracts); TfL + Oyster ridership; OS AddressBase / Land Registry.
 • Amsterdam / Netherlands — KvK business register + BAG building/address cadastre; and CBS publishes gridded population at 100 m. Note the 2026-09-09 correction: this used to be scored as removing Loci's most error-prone step, but D38 already retired the tract→hex dasymetric interpolation in NYC — demographics now join tract → address directly, with no apportionment and the tract MOE carried as-is. Gridded population is therefore a convenience for a city with no address file, not the upgrade over the NYC pipeline this dossier originally claimed; where an address or building register exists (BAG here, AddressBase in the UK), that is the better match to how Loci actually works.
 • Tokyo / Japan — Economic Census of establishments by industry (near-census) + e-Stat census on 250/500 m mesh (gridded). Weakness: OSM/Overture POI coverage is thinner.
 • Chicago (and SF / LA / Seattle-King County / Boston / DC) — nearly free US ports: ACS, LODES, SNAP, FDIC come with the country. Chicago's all-industry business-LICENSE file is a stronger anchor than DOHMH's food-only census.
 • Toronto / Vancouver, Sydney / Melbourne, Singapore, Stockholm / Copenhagen / Helsinki / Berlin — register-based or fine-census societies; note footprint (Singapore is one small city-state) and anchor specifics.

The one-line finding to preserve: the gating asset is the unbiased anchor, and on that axis France (SIRENE), the Netherlands (KvK+CBS grid), the UK (FSA+Companies House) and Chicago (business licenses) are at least as good as NYC — several ALSO hand you gridded population, which the US does not — though see the correction above on how much that is now worth.

Reframed 2026-09-09 (D38): the tract→hex dasymetric step this dossier scored cities against no longer exists; rescored on address/building registers instead. E8 remains parked at Low per D46 — this is a wording fix, not a scheduling change.

Title: Generic near-census anchor adapter interface
Description: Generalize the NYC anchor concept (DOHMH/SNAP/SLA as near-census calibration sources, CONTEXT §7.1) into a pluggable adapter contract, so a second city's SIRENE / FSA / Companies House / municipal business-license file lands in the SAME staging.poi contract carrying the `anchor` flag the coverage-bias calibration already consumes. This is the piece that makes the whole coverage-bias mitigation portable rather than NYC-only — without it, a second city has the biased OSM/Overture layer but nothing unbiased to calibrate it against, and the P3 threat is un-mitigable there. Interface only in this milestone; the concrete per-city adapters are follow-on ingest tickets once a pilot city is chosen.

Title: Gridded-population adapter (skip dasymetric where a grid exists)
Description:
For the cities that publish population on a native fine grid — NL CBS 100 m, Japan e-Stat mesh, Nordic and German (Zensus) grids — consume the grid directly into hex_demographics instead of running the tract→hex dasymetric interpolation (E1's most error-prone step, the one carrying ACS MOEs and the parks/rail-yards smearing risk). This is a genuine QUALITY UPGRADE over the NYC pipeline, not just a port: gridded input removes the largest single source of interpolation error. Build as an alternative demographics path selected by the CITIES rubric's land_use=3 flag.

CANCELED 2026-09-09 (CHECKPOINT D38/D46, Linear GTM-91): the ticket's entire value was skipping the tract→hex dasymetric interpolation, and that step no longer exists — D38 made the residential ADDRESS the unit, so demographics join tract → address directly with no apportionment and the tract MOE carried as-is. There is no interpolation left for a gridded input to remove, and a population grid is the wrong shape for the address unit anyway: it would re-introduce apportionment (grid cell → addresses) to replace a step that was already eliminated. What a second city actually needs is an address or building register (BAG, AddressBase), which is a different ticket and belongs to the parked E8 checklist (GTM-104). Compounding it, D46 parks second-city work at Low indefinitely. No address-level equivalent worth keeping open.

Title: Pick the first pilot city + coverage-warning report
Description: Recommend ONE city to run first, with the trade stated: Chicago is the cheapest port (US federal data free, all-industry license anchor) and the fastest way to prove city-agnosticism; London or Paris is the strongest demonstration that the method travels internationally and that the anchor can be even better than NYC's. Whichever is chosen, produce the coverage-warning report the E5 second-city ticket requires: per daily-needs category, does this city have an unbiased anchor, or does that category run on OSM/Overture alone (and therefore inherit the §7.1 undercount)? The report is the honesty artifact — it says exactly where the second-city gap screen is trustworthy and where it is not.

Title: SHIP: second-city feasibility scorecard
Description: Milestone deliverable: a ranked scorecard of candidate cities across the four rubric axes (anchor / land-use / demographics / transit), each cell naming the concrete dataset and its 0–3 score, min-gated so the anchor dominates. Headline the recommended pilot and the reasoning. This is a decision artifact for the owner, not a public memo — it answers 'where do we take Loci next, and what will it cost to get the data there.' Load the `dataviz` skill before writing chart code.

Title: Catalyst-anchored pre-ignition screen (loci ignition)
Description:
Since ignition is not in a neighborhood's own trajectory (D25) and a naive PLUTO headroom score just surfaces low-density suburbs (D26), screen for PRE-IGNITION on the exogenous project pipeline instead: a curated CATALYST layer (committed transit / rezonings / megaprojects) × low-mid maturity × a light urban-density floor.

Two design lessons baked in: requiring a real catalyst IS the suburb-filter (so the density floor stays LOW or it wrongly drops low-rise-but-catalyzed frontiers like East New York); and the screen's no-catalyst reject list is honest QA for catalysts the layer is missing.

DONE 2026-09-02 — src/loci/model/ignition.py + `loci ignition`. 44 candidates; East Harlem N (SAS Ph2 + rezoning) is the flagship, converging with the independent trajectory work. See CHECKPOINT D26 / QUESTIONS O5.

Title: DOB new-building corroboration layer
Description:
Is development ACTUALLY happening at a candidate, or is the catalyst just paper? Pull DOB new-building filings, geocode to NTA × year, and attach a recent-activity column to the screen.

DONE 2026-09-02 — 198,514 NB filings (classic ic3t-wcy2) geocoded to NTA×year 2000–2023 (scratchpad/nb_by_nta_year.json); `loci ignition` now shows NB18-23 per candidate. It separates real building (East New York 253, Crown Heights 215, Ocean Hill 151, East Harlem 118) from stalled (Two Bridges 14). KNOWN GAP: ic3t-wcy2 undercounts post-2016 (DOB NOW migration) — see the DOB-NOW union ticket.

Title: Catalyst→change lag study (the two-clock finding)
Description:
Owner question: how long between a catalyst and completion / human-behavior change? Event study of dated past catalysts against DOB permits and the maturity panel (`loci ignition --lag`).

DONE 2026-09-02 — TWO CLOCKS: catalyst→construction ~5–9 yr (permit surge, peak ~6–11 yr, clean on the 2003–09 catalysts); catalyst→demographic tip 10–20 yr, sustained, and ONLY if market-rate — East New York (affordable-dominated, 2016) built the most yet gentrified BELOW the citywide drift (densified without tipping, confirming D21). Product read: construction/land play is this cycle; appreciation play is 2030s–40s and conditional on catalyst type. CHECKPOINT D27, report ignition_lag_findings.md.

Title: Union DOB NOW to fix the post-2016 permit undercount
Description: The classic DOB dataset (ic3t-wcy2) was superseded by DOB NOW (`w9ak-ipjd`) around 2016, so recent new-building filings are undercounted — which is exactly the window the forward catalysts live in, making the recent construction-lag numbers unreliable. Union DOB NOW with the classic set (dedup on job/BIN), re-geocode to NTA × year, and re-run the corroboration + lag. This is what lets the recent catalysts (East Harlem, Atlantic Ave) get a trustworthy construction-response read.

Title: Diff-in-diff: catalyst effect vs matched controls
Description:
The lag study is a descriptive event study — and catalysts cluster in already-rising areas, which is the SAME endogeneity that sank the §0 causal thesis. Move from timing toward causation: match each catalyzed NTA to controls on pre-catalyst maturity, trajectory, transit and borough, and estimate a difference-in-differences on maturity and on new-building activity around the catalyst year.

Mandatory honesty per the project's standard: report the pre-trend (do treated and control move in parallel BEFORE the catalyst?), and state plainly if parallel trends fails — a catalyst that lands where growth was already coming is not a proven cause. Do NOT let the retail residual enter (D1).

Title: Expand the catalyst layer from DCP ZAP / MTA capital / EDC
Description:
The catalyst layer is hand-curated (28 projects) and demonstrably incomplete — the screen's own no-catalyst reject list surfaces real urban candidates whose catalysts are missing (Chinatown-Two Bridges was added after it appeared; Harlem-125th, Washington Heights still open). Systematize it: pull adopted + pending rezonings from DCP ZAP, funded/planned transit from the MTA capital program, and megaprojects from EDC/ESD, each with a date and status. Promote the CATALYSTS list to package data (a registry-style file), not an in-module literal.

The reject list is the acceptance test: after the pull, the high-headroom urban no-catalyst set should shrink to genuinely un-catalyzed places.

Title: Validate adjacency-diffusion as a distinct ignition channel
Description: Catalysts are one exogenous channel; spatial diffusion from the already-risen frontier (Williamsburg → Bed-Stuy → Bushwick → Crown Heights → Ocean Hill → East New York, O5) is another. Test whether adjacency to a high-maturity NTA predicts a subsequent maturity rise AFTER controlling for having a catalyst — i.e. does 'next to the frontier' add signal beyond 'has a rezoning'? If yes, add an adjacency term to the ignition score; if the two are collinear (catalysts land next to the frontier), say so.

Title: Productionize the ignition layer (package data + DB)
Description: ignition.py currently reads the maturity panel and the NB layer from hard-coded scratchpad paths and keeps the catalyst list as an in-module literal — fine for the spike, not for reproducibility (acceptance criterion C). Persist analysis.nta_trajectory and analysis.nb_by_nta_year into the DuckDB, move CATALYSTS to package data, drop the scratchpad paths, and add a unit test on the screen (a catalyst-less suburb must NOT appear; a low-rise catalyzed frontier MUST). Wire into `make check`.

Title: Relabel the Arrival Curve artifact as ranking / scenario
Description: The 2033 backtest (O4/D25) showed the projection fails as a point forecast — it ships as ranking + scenario only. The published Arrival Curve still frames the 2033 arrows as a forecast. Update the artifact copy (arrows = trajectory ranking / scenario, not a prediction) and add a one-line note that ignition timing is exogenous and lagged (the two-clock finding), so the visual matches what the backtest actually licenses.

Title: Category-expansion mechanics: the fail-closed checklist for a 16th slug
Description:
URGENT because it is the check that decides whether every other E10 ticket is valid, and because the codebase already fails closed in four places — a slug added to `categories.py` without its five yaml rows breaks the suite on the next test run. Write the checklist ONCE, here, instead of rediscovering it six times.

The surfaces a new category must land on, all verified present in the code: `categories.py` CATEGORIES + a TIER assignment; `categories.yaml` (naics_2022, naics_2017, label, per-source vocab — D42); `reach_tiers.yaml` (reach_m + basis + justification + citations — D41; `reach.load_reach` raises on a missing category); `conveniences.yaml` (owner_m/owner_min, the fallback reach_tiers reads); `demand.yaml`/`spend.yaml` (the class is DERIVED from a CEX income_elasticity at the 0.35 cut — D49; `demand.load_demand` and `tests/test_demand_caveat.py` (b2) both fail on a category with no elasticity, so THERE IS NO WAY to add a category without sourcing a real CEX line); `zbp_naics.yaml` (NAICS 2017 + confidence; `zbp.py` raises on a missing category); `benchmarks.yaml`; the adapter vocab maps (osm_overpass, overture_places, foursquare_places) and the D52(a) supply-set anchor list; the Google validation type map (`tests/test_google_types_drift.py`); the webmap legend and `viz/webmap_export.py`; and CONTEXT.md §2.1's human table, which is the docs-drift half of the CLAUDE.md 'machine-check the docs against the code' habit.

THREE CONSEQUENCES TO PRICE BEFORE ANY ADD LANDS, because they move numbers that are already published:
 • `TIER_WEIGHTS` (0.40/0.20/0.25/0.15) is a partition over 15 slugs. Six more slugs re-weight every DNCI value ever computed. Decide whether DNCI is re-stated or whether the expansion is scoped to the address screen only.
 • `address_gaps.MIN_PRESENT` is the literal 12 of '≥12 of 15'. With 21 categories it is either 12/21 (much looser) or re-derived. D51 already found the gate does no work inside MN+BK (100% MN, 95% BK eligible), so re-derive it and say so rather than leaving a magic constant.
 • `gap_score = max ratio` (D41) is monotone in the number of categories: adding six can only raise each address's score and can move `lead`, for reasons unrelated to new evidence at that address. Report the before/after distribution per category, description-style, never as a top-N list (D52 rule).

Deliverable: a `loci check-categories` subcommand (a CLI subcommand, not a loose script — CLAUDE.md) that asserts every slug in CATEGORIES appears in all seven yamls, every naics_2022 code exists in naics_2022.csv, every naics_2017 code appears in the live CBP vocabulary, and that CONTEXT §2.1's table matches categories.yaml. It should fail today if any of that is untrue.

Pushed to Linear 2026-09-09 as GTM-112 (Urgent priority).

Title: Add `dentist` — NPPES anchor (NYS Office of the Professions is NOT usable)
Description:
NAICS 2022 621210 Offices of Dentists (unchanged from 2017). Highest prevalence of any candidate: 190 establishments across ten MN+BK ZIPs (CBP 2023) — above coin laundry, above liquor, second only to grocery/bar/pharmacy among everything measured.

VERIFICATION THAT CHANGES THE PLAN: the assumed anchor, the NYS Office of the Professions, DOES NOT WORK. op.nysed.gov publishes no bulk licensee file — only an online verification search over ~1.5M licensees — and its record is person-level with city and state but NO practice street address. Anchoring on it is impossible, and that finding kills the same assumption for eye care and vets.

Use NPPES instead (CMS National Plan and Provider Enumeration System): free, bulk-downloadable (download.cms.gov/nppes/NPI_Files.html, verified 200) with a keyless API (npiregistry.cms.hhs.gov/api/?version=2.1) that returns practice-LOCATION street addresses filterable by taxonomy and ZIP — probed live against a NYC ZIP and it returned dentist offices with address_purpose LOCATION. Filter to the 122300000X dentist taxonomy family. Register it in registry.yaml as a universal-tier anchor (it is national, so it also improves the E8 second-city story).

MEASURE COVERAGE BEFORE TRUSTING IT: NPPES is a PROVIDER registry, not an establishment registry — several dentists share one address, so counts must be collapsed by address first, the same failure mode D52(b) fixed for the 996 booth-renter nails licences at a shared coordinate. Only after that collapse is the NPPES/ZBP ratio meaningful, and only if it clears 0.7 does the D52(a) supply-set rule let lone-aggregator records be excluded.

reach: no walk standard exists — the dental-access literature is HPSA population-to-provider RATIOS, the same shape D41 already rejected for childcare. `basis: none`, owner norm; proposed 1,200 m, since a dental visit is a booked, infrequent trip people travel further for.
demand: CEX 'Dental services' is a clean 1:1 Table 1101 line; expect necessity. Set `reliable: false` on the spend row for the pharmacy reason (T5): revenue is substantially third-party-payer, so a household-budget spend model is wrong in SHAPE, not merely noisy.
zbp: dentist → 621210, confidence high.

Pushed to Linear 2026-09-09 as GTM-113.

Title: Add `specialty_food` (butcher / fish / produce / non-cafe bakery)
Description:
NAICS 2022 445240 Meat Retailers, 445250 Fish and Seafood Retailers, 445230 Fruit and Vegetable Retailers, 445291 Baked Goods Retailers (2017: 445210, 445220, 445230, 445291 — read out of the real concordance file). 119 establishments across ten MN+BK ZIPs (CBP 2023), split meat 39 / produce 30 / fish 29 / baked 21.

Anchor: NYS Department of Agriculture and Markets **Retail Food Stores**, data.ny.gov `9a8c-vfzj` — verified live: 11,472 NYC rows (KINGS 4,254, QUEENS 2,542, BRONX 2,235, NEW YORK 1,921, RICHMOND 520), point geometry, plus a `square_footage` column that is directly useful to the O7/O8 fair-price work. It licences EVERY retail food store in the state, so it is a near-census candidate for all four sub-formats and a second opinion on `grocery` and `convenience` besides.

FIRST TASK, AND THE WHOLE RISK: decode `estab_type`. The values are letter combinations (Kings: AC 3,364, A 624, ABC 81, ABCH 52, ACH 33 …) whose legend is a PDF at data.ny.gov/api/views/9a8c-vfzj/files/UBDP3oW2f-K767I4f51EJaIUO8eNGPrAQQj8tSvBhbo (HTTP 200, NOT yet parsed). If those codes separate a butcher from a bodega, RFS is a real anchor. If they do not, the fallback is `dba_name` keyword classification, which is materially weaker and must be reported as such — do not let a keyword match be described as an anchor.

BOUNDARY COLLISION, NOT A COVERAGE PROBLEM: `shop=greengrocer` and Overture `farmers_market` currently count as `grocery`, and `shop=bakery` / Overture `bakery` count as `cafe_bakery`. Adding this category therefore REMOVES supply from two existing categories and will move their gap counts for no new evidence. Sequence it before any run that quotes grocery or cafe_bakery numbers, and report before/after per category as a description, never a top-N list (D52). The seated-cafe vs takeaway-bakery split has no clean signal in any feed — state that rather than implying the split is measured.

reach: `basis: analog` — grocery's cited 800 m (USDA FARA 0.5 mi / NYC FRESH / Portland's 20-minute neighborhood). Honest caveat in the justification: no source names specialty food, and a butcher is plausibly a longer trip than a supermarket.
demand: CEX food-at-home sub-lines exist for all four (meats/poultry/fish/eggs; fresh fruits and vegetables; bakery products), with NY MSA figures in Table 3004. Expect ~0.35, i.e. right ON the D49 cut — this row is the most likely of the six to flip class, so choose the sub-line deliberately and record which one and why.
zbp: specialty_food → 445210 + 445220 + 445230 + 445291, all confidence high.

Title: Add `eye_care` (optometrists + optical goods)
Description:
NAICS 2022 621320 Offices of Optometrists + 456130 Optical Goods Retailers (2017: 621320 + 446130 — the 446→456 recode is the same health-and-personal-care renumbering that moved pharmacy in D42). 94 establishments across ten MN+BK ZIPs (optical goods 49, optometrists 45).

HALF-ANCHORED, and the ticket should say so on the artifact: NPPES covers the clinical half (taxonomy 152W00000X, optometrists) with practice-location addresses; the RETAIL half has no anchor at all — eyewear shops are unlicensed retail and DCWP does not license them (verified against the 46 active DCWP business_category values in w7w3-xahh, which contain no optician, pharmacy, laundry or pet category). Under D52(a) the category keeps all canonical records until that changes.

Title: Add `dollar_variety` (dollar and variety stores)
Description:
NAICS 2022 455219 All Other General Merchandise Retailers (2017: 452319). 97 establishments across ten MN+BK ZIPs — real prevalence, comparable to drycleaning.

NO ANCHOR. DCWP does not license general merchandise (verified). The only partial coverage is that dollar stores selling packaged food appear in the NYS Retail Food Stores roster (9a8c-vfzj), which is biased to the food-selling subset — usable as a corroboration source, not as an anchor. Under D52(a) this category therefore keeps every canonical record including lone-aggregator ones, which is exactly the population D40/D47 identified as the overcount, so it will look better-supplied than it is. Publish its POI/ZBP ratio with the first run.

reach: `basis: none`, owner norm. Proposed 960 m — the stock-up errand tier the owner gave `hardware`, not a daily-needs tier.
demand: no single CEX line; the honest mapping is a blend of 'Housekeeping supplies' and 'Miscellaneous household products', so mark `reliable: false` the way `convenience` already is rather than dressing a blend as a citation. Expect ~0.2 → necessity.
zbp: dollar_variety → 452319, confidence MEDIUM — 452319 also holds non-dollar general merchandise, so the code is broader than the category.

'No dollar store here' does not read as an opportunity the way 'no pharmacy here' does — consider whether this belongs in the DNCI bundle at all or ships as a context layer.

Title: Add `vet_pet` (veterinary + pet supply) — last, and with a coverage warning
Description:
NAICS 2022 541940 Veterinary Services + 459910 Pet and Pet Supplies Retailers (2017: 541940 + 453910). 51 establishments across ten MN+BK ZIPs (vet 34, pet supply 17) — the thinnest of the six adds.

NO ANCHOR EXISTS, and three candidate anchors were checked and eliminated: the NYS Office of the Professions licenses veterinarians but publishes no bulk file and no practice address; NPPES does not help because veterinarians are not NPI-eligible (they are not HIPAA-covered providers); and data.ny.gov has no pet-dealer or veterinary licensing dataset (catalog searches for 'pet' and 'veterinary' return nothing relevant). That leaves Overture + Foursquare + OSM only. D52(a)'s rule for an unanchored category is 'all canonical records stay, and loading the anchor is the fix' — here there is no anchor to load, so the fix is unavailable and the coverage caveat is permanent until one appears.

Order it LAST for that reason: no anchor + lowest prevalence is the combination most likely to manufacture gap flags that are really feed thinness, which is the D40/D47 failure mode this project already knows it has.

reach: `basis: none`, owner norm; proposed 1,200 m for the combined slug.
demand: CEX has a real 'Pets' line (Table 1101); expect ~0.45 → DISCRETIONARY, so its gaps carry the demand caveat.
zbp: vet_pet → 541940 (high) + 453910 (high).
risk, and the reason to consider splitting: the slug fuses two different behaviours under one reach value — a booked medical appointment people will travel for, and a heavy carry-home supply run they will not. If the owner will accept a seventeenth slug, splitting is more defensible than a compromise distance that is wrong for both.

Pushed to Linear 2026-09-09 as GTM-117.

Title: Fix the coverage validator's local counts and .env loading
Description:
`_local_counts` read UN-deduplicated staging.poi and looked up only 'overture_places' plus a never-ingested 'osm_overpass', so foursquare_os_places — the dominant source for hardware, fitness and clinic — was silently dropped from every local count. That biases the validator in its one dangerous direction: loci's own supply is understated, so the comparison drifts toward 'Google can see businesses loci cannot', which is precisely the conclusion the harness exists to TEST rather than assume.

Fix: new column `n_local_canonical` (canonical, deduplicated, all sources) on analysis.coverage_validation, plus `loci validate --recount-local` to backfill existing rows without spending a single Google call — the ledger was the binding constraint, so a re-run was not an option. Also fixed: the CLI now loads loci/.env via python-dotenv (override=False); GOOGLE_PLACES_KEY set in .env had been invisible and `--run` failed outright.

Title: Ship the reach rule and its monotonicity test; reject the p80 calibration
Description:
Implements the D33 redefinition: `rule="reach"` in model/gaps.py (`_compute_gaps_reach`, shared `_eligible_universe` gate), `reach.py` + `reach.yaml` (per-category reach = p80 of hex-to-nearest-c network distance over populated hexes), `loci gaps --rule reach` writing analysis.hex_gaps_reach (the window rule and analysis.hex_gaps left untouched as history), `loci reach-table`, and tests/test_gaps_monotonicity.py. Verified: `loci reach-table` reproduces reach.yaml exactly; the reach rule gives 1,707 gap hexes / 6,189 hex-category pairs vs 726 hexes under the window rule; scaling every reach by 0.8 yields a strict SUPERSET (2,251 hexes / 10,783 pairs) — monotonicity holds on production data, not only in the unit test.

The calibration is rejected, and that is the point of the ticket: p80 of the hex-to-nearest distribution makes ~20% of eligible hexes a gap for EVERY category by construction, so per-category counts are flat (childcare 460, tailor 446, grocery 433, restaurant 427, hardware 368, bank 367) and the rule cannot say which business NYC is short of. 56% of eligible hexes are gaps; only 468 (15%) miss exactly one category while 888 miss three or more. The exactly-one list is a quantile artifact — stable in SIZE across p70/p80/p90 (463/468/471) but not in membership (p80∩p70 = 152/468, p80∩p90 = 95/468). `lead = min(missing, key=reach)` is a fixed global priority list: restaurant (275 m) leads 427 hexes whose nearest restaurant is a median 352 m away. And the flag is largely a coverage flag: corr(n_missing, log POI count within 800 m) = −0.67.

What is kept: the reach ARCHITECTURE (a fixed per-category distance, no global window, monotone) and the monotonicity acceptance test. What is dropped: the p80 quantile as the calibration statistic and the min-reach lead rule. Also fixed: build_gaps' return annotation (was `-> int`, returns a tuple).

Title: Compare reach calibrations: same-type spacing, p80, and external walk-time tiers
Description:
The D34 rejection left the calibration statistic open. All candidates were run through the unchanged `compute_gaps(rule="reach")` over the 3,041 eligible hexes so that only the reach table varied.

Results: (a) same-type store-to-store spacing is dead on arrival — NYC same-type nearest-neighbour spacing is 0–218 m at the median (restaurant 0, nails 0, grocery 22, hardware 218) because a trade's stores share a block; it measures CLUSTERING, not a service radius, and yields 3,041/3,041 gap hexes with a single exactly-one hex. (b) p80 on all populated hexes and (c) p80 refit on the gated universe are the tautology: per-category gap-count CV 0.063 and 0.003, every category 605–612, exactly 20% under c. (d) External tiers by trip frequency — 400 m grocery/convenience/pharmacy/cafe_bakery/restaurant/childcare, 800 m laundry/bar/fitness/hair_barber/nails_beauty, 1,200 m bank/clinic/hardware/tailor_repair — is the only candidate whose per-category counts carry information (CV 1.07, range 0–771), the most stable under a ±10% perturbation (Jaccard 0.54), and has the least marginal leads (median excess 125 m). Totals for (d): 1,689 gap hexes, 730 exactly-one.

Lead rule: min-reach must go (it ties on 42% of hexes under any tiered reach and is then decided by dict order); max-ratio (nearest_m / reach_m) beats max-excess, because raw metres reward whichever category has the widest reach. Monotonicity holds for every candidate (reach×0.8 removes 0 pairs) — it is the rule's property, not the calibration's, and therefore proves nothing about the calibration.

What no calibration fixes, and what the artifact must say: corr(n_missing, log POI count within 800 m) stays −0.62 to −0.70 for all of them, so 'missing' is still largely 'low retail density'. The tier ASSIGNMENT is now the load-bearing choice — moving pharmacy 400→800 drops it 763→21 gaps and childcare 771→60, and reassigning two tiers overlaps the exactly-one list only 347/988 — so the tiers must be pinned to a citable external source or explicitly to owner norms.

Title: Diagnose 0 m same-type spacing: graph snapping vs DOHMH turnover
Description:
The D35 spacing run found restaurant and nails_beauty at a MEDIAN 0 m same-type network distance. If that were real duplication it would bias every nearest-distance in the gap screen low, so it had to be resolved before any spacing-based calibration could be trusted.

Straight-line check: 74.5% of restaurants share a walk-graph node with another restaurant, but WITHIN those '0 m network' pairs the straight-line distance is a median 16.4 m (p90 47 m, max 134 m) — so ~86% of the 0 m result is the walk graph being coarser than storefront spacing, not the data. The residual true-zero share (13–14% of restaurant, nails_beauty and clinic canonical POIs at an identical coordinate) traces to `sources/cities/nyc/dohmh.py`: it dedupes by CAMIS but never filters closed establishments out of DOHMH's 3-year rolling inspection window, so a closed tenant and its successor at one address both survive as canonical points. Cross-source legal-vs-trade name confusion is NOT the driver — only 0.09% of ≤15 m restaurant pairs share a normalized name.

Impact on the gap screen is minimal (duplicates share a coordinate and a category, so nearest-distance is unchanged); the real exposure is inflated raw counts feeding the DNCI saturating term in well-served food and beauty hexes. Actions: filter the DOHMH adapter to currently-active establishments before dedup, reconcile the score/dedup.py docstring (says 25 m) against MATCH_METERS = 40.0, and treat network-0 m spacing as uninformative for calibration. No change to the name-matching dedup logic.

Title: Address-level reach screen: fixed eligibility gate and a continuous ranking
Description:
The port of the reach rule to the address geography, run over 767,337 residential addresses / 3,735,269 units with per-address nearest distance for all 15 categories from the conveniences Dijkstra engine (158 s).

The finding that decides the design: the LITERAL port — eligible iff within reach of ≥12/15 categories, gap iff nearest beyond reach — VIOLATES monotonicity for every candidate calibration, because reach×0.8 removes 209k–232k gap pairs as addresses fall out of eligibility faster than they gain gaps. That is the D33 defect re-introduced at a new geography. Gating instead on a FIXED, reach-INDEPENDENT presence test (≤800 m for ≥12/15, as gaps.py's `_eligible_universe` already does) restores it: 0 pairs removed for all candidates. Rule to hold: the eligibility gate must never depend on the reach table. Fixed gate yields 607,245 eligible addresses (79.1% of addresses, 90.7% of units).

Second finding: the 'exactly one missing' list is unstable at EVERY geography — ±10% reach gives Jaccard 0.41–0.58 against the D34 bar of ≥80%. That is a structural property of a binary knife-edge classification, not of any calibration, so the deliverable ranks addresses by a CONTINUOUS statistic (max nearest/reach ratio, or the lead's excess over reach) and does not publish a binary list. Also recorded: coverage correlation persists (−0.58 to −0.65); top clusters by units are single mega-lots (Co-op City towers, 10,914 and 9,669 units on one PLUTO lot), so clustering must be by building/lot group with a unit cap or the ranking is a housing-density list; Jaccard with the legacy 800 m/80% address output is 0.24 and that output is superseded.
